prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker is deeply infatuated with someone who remains emotionally distant and unavailable.
- Brief memories and fleeting glimpses of the person sustain the speaker’s longing without providing resolution.
- The speaker feels that their ambitions and practical plans collapse whenever they remember the person’s voice.
- The speaker wishes the attraction were mutual but recognizes that the connection may exist mostly in their imagination.
- Despite repeated avoidance and disappointment, the speaker continues to look for chances to encounter the person.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores unrequited longing and romantic obsession through a speaker’s ornate, French-inflected monologue of missed encounters, imagined meanings, and thwarted attempts at closeness. It reveals that the beloved’s absence dominates and diminishes the speaker’s life, making every glimpse feel significant while leaving the desire permanently unresolved.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Though, The, Each

outputs.L1:
Though it is all too clear how unimpressed you are by a *cri de cœur*, and though wafting away unhugged is, from your perspective, *de rigueur*, I remain a restless entrepreneur of schemes to rendezvous with you.

The thought of you converts my favorite main dishes into *hors d’œuvres*. My addiction to the tingling you induce is a *fait accompli*. Each drifting day is another page in the secret book whose *dénouement* never arrives, while your fleeting glances lock me into this unfinishable *roman à clef*. The idea that any one remembered moment at a party or picnic was my sole, forever-lost chance to touch you must be a *cul-de-sac*.

When my projects for a prudent career try to stand, your remembered voice administers the *coup de grâce*, and my *mélange* of bright ideas becomes a mere *potpourri*. How I would love to believe this dance is a *folie à deux*. The way you stride across Memorial Drive is a *tour de force*, but glimpses across traffic make a paper-thin *raison d’être*. Your recent exit is implicit in many a *mise en scène*. It is as if you heard me approaching for a *tête-à-tête* and slipped into the elevator with your tall boots and *sangfroid*. Always, you get to *reculer*, and I never seem to *mieux sauter*—

Still, I will keep an eye out for you on every *rez-de-chaussée*.
outputs.L2:
Although your lack of response to my heartfelt plea could hardly be more obvious, and although drifting off without an embrace seems, to you, the proper etiquette for avoiding any arranged meeting with me, I remain an agitated schemer. Thinking of you reduces even my most beloved entrées to appetizers. My dependence on the electric sensation you create is already settled beyond dispute.

Every aimless day becomes one more sheet in a hidden volume whose ending never comes, and your brief looks trap me inside a roman à clef that cannot be completed. The notion that some single remembered instant at a party or a picnic was my one vanished opportunity to reach for you has to be a dead end.

Whenever my sensible professional ambitions attempt to rise, the recollection of your voice delivers the fatal blow, and my assortment of promising plans collapses into nothing more than a fragrant miscellany. How gladly I would persuade myself that this dance belongs to both of us, a shared madness. Your walk across Memorial Drive is a stunning performance, but catching sight of you through the traffic offers only the thinnest possible reason for being.

Your latest departure is suggested in scene after scene. It is almost as though, sensing me draw near for a private conversation, you stepped into the elevator in your high boots and perfect composure. You are always able to step back, while I never quite manage to leap better afterward. Even so, I will continue watching for you on every ground floor.
outputs.L3:
The speaker is overwhelmed by a deep infatuation for someone who remains emotionally distant and unavailable. This person occupies a powerful place in the speaker’s thoughts, yet there is little evidence of real closeness or reciprocity. The attraction feels intense and consuming, but it is met with silence, absence, or indifference, leaving the speaker caught between desire and uncertainty.

What keeps this longing alive are brief memories and fleeting glimpses. A passing sight, a remembered expression, or a momentary encounter is enough to renew the speaker’s feelings. These fragments do not bring comfort or resolution; instead, they prolong the emotional tension. The speaker survives on small impressions, treating them almost as proof of a connection, even though they offer no clear promise of anything more.

The person’s voice has a particularly destabilizing effect. Whenever the speaker remembers it, their ambitions, routines, and practical plans seem to collapse. Goals that once felt important lose their urgency, and ordinary responsibilities become difficult to sustain. The memory of the voice interrupts the speaker’s sense of direction, pulling them away from rational decisions and back into longing.

At the same time, the speaker is aware of the painful imbalance in the situation. They wish the attraction were mutual and hope that the other person might feel something similar. However, they also recognize that much of the connection may exist mainly in their own imagination. This awareness creates an inner conflict: the speaker wants to believe in the possibility of shared feeling, but they cannot ignore the likelihood that they are projecting meaning onto distant or ambiguous moments.

Despite repeated disappointment and the other person’s continued avoidance, the speaker cannot fully let go. They continue to seek out opportunities for accidental meetings, shared spaces, or brief exchanges. Even when experience suggests that nothing will change, the hope of another encounter remains difficult to resist. The result is a cycle of longing, frustration, and renewed expectation, in which the speaker remains emotionally attached to someone who may never truly be available.
outputs.L4:
The speaker’s monologue unfolds as an elaborate confession of unrequited longing, shaped by romantic obsession and by the pain of never being fully seen by the beloved. The language is ornate, self-conscious, and French-inflected, giving the voice an air of refinement while also emphasizing its theatrical intensity. The speaker does not simply describe affection; they transform every glance, every possible meeting, and every accidental nearness into a charged emotional event. Ordinary moments become symbolic, as if the beloved’s smallest gesture might contain a hidden message or promise.

Much of the text is built around missed encounters and frustrated possibilities. The speaker imagines meanings where there may be none, revisiting brief glimpses and passing impressions as though they could be rearranged into proof of intimacy. Their desire depends less on actual closeness than on anticipation, memory, and fantasy. Because the beloved remains distant, the speaker fills the silence with interpretation, turning absence into a kind of presence. The beloved is not fully known as a person but becomes an object of projection, a figure onto whom the speaker casts hope, disappointment, and longing.

This obsession gradually reveals the imbalance at the heart of the speaker’s emotional life. The beloved’s absence dominates everything, making the speaker’s own existence feel diminished and dependent. Every encounter, however fleeting, seems momentous, while every failure to connect deepens the sense of deprivation. The speaker’s world narrows around the beloved, so that desire becomes both sustaining and destructive. It gives life intensity, but it also prevents resolution, trapping the speaker in a cycle of expectation and defeat.

Ultimately, the text presents longing as something that cannot be satisfied because it is rooted in distance. The speaker seeks closeness, recognition, and perhaps love, yet the beloved remains unreachable. The ornate style of the monologue mirrors this emotional excess: it beautifies the suffering while also exposing its futility. What remains is a portrait of desire suspended in uncertainty, where each glimpse seems meaningful but no meaning is ever confirmed, and where romantic obsession continues precisely because fulfillment never arrives.
outputs.L5:
**Though**, **the**, and **each** are small words, but they play important roles in English.

**Though** is often used to show contrast. For example: “Though it was raining, we went for a walk.” It helps connect two ideas that seem different or surprising.

**The** is a definite article. It points to something specific, such as “the book,” “the sun,” or “the answer.” It tells the reader or listener that we are talking about a particular thing.

**Each** refers to individual members of a group. For example: “Each student received a notebook.” It emphasizes that every person or item is considered separately.

Though these words may seem simple, the meaning of a sentence can change greatly depending on how each one is used.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lovesick prose poem addressed to an unattainable person, using as many French loanwords and phrases as possible (cri de cœur, de rigueur, rendezvous, fait accompli, roman à clef, cul de sac, coup de grâce, etc.) and set it around a city/campus scene like Memorial Drive and elevators.
counterfactuals.output:
You, impossible *mon amour*, are always across Memorial Drive when the light changes—there in the autumn *clair de lune* of traffic, beneath the sycamores shedding their little *souvenirs*, your scarf a blue *accent aigu* against the gray campus air. I stand on my side of the boulevard, all *ennui* and *désir*, pretending to read the posters for colloquia and film series, when really every announcement is a *roman à clef* in which you are the secret protagonist and I am the marginal note, the *hors d’œuvre* left untouched.

To love you is my *cri de cœur*, my private *folie à deux* without the courtesy of the second participant. You pass with your coffee, your books, your immaculate *savoir-faire*, and the day arranges itself around you as if your existence were *de rigueur*. Even the buses kneel. Even the Charles—or whatever river of light and exhaust runs beside us—seems to murmur *c’est la vie* in a voice too elegant to pity me.

We have shared elevators, yes, those vertical little *salons* of fluorescent intimacy, where the floor numbers ascend like improbable hopes: 3, 4, 5, 6. Your shoulder near mine, your perfume a delicate *je ne sais quoi*, my heartbeat making a scandalous *faux pas* in my chest. Once you said, “Excuse me,” and it was a *rendezvous* to me, a treaty, a *fait accompli*. I stepped aside as though granting passage to royalty, as though my whole life had been a narrow *cul-de-sac* designed solely for that moment when you would need to exit.

Ah, how ridiculous, how *très chic* in misery I have become. I wander the Infinite Corridor of my longing, past bulletin boards and glass doors, past laboratories humming with more practical miracles, carrying my heart like a contraband *objet d’art*. Every glimpse of you is an *aperçu* of paradise; every absence, the *coup de grâce*. Your name in my mouth is a forbidden *amuse-bouche*. Your laughter, overheard near the vending machines, is the *pièce de résistance* of the afternoon.

And yet you remain unattainable, *bien sûr*—not cruel, never cruel, only elsewhere. You are the thesis I cannot defend, the password I cannot guess, the locked office after hours, the elevator already closing while I hurry across the lobby with all my tender *déjà vu*. I press the button again and again, but the machinery of fate has no *merci* in it.

So I offer you this little *billet-doux*, this campus nocturne, this pedestrian *confession intime* from the far curb of Memorial Drive. Take nothing from it, *ma chère*, except perhaps the faint knowledge that somewhere between the crosswalk and the elevators, between the lecture hall and the river’s cold *bravura*, someone has made of your absence a cathedral, of your indifference a weather, of your passing shadow a whole impossible *raison d’être*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single breathless paragraph in the voice of an obsessive admirer who keeps missing chances to speak to someone, with every sentence incorporating a common French expression used in English.
counterfactuals.output: Every morning I see you at the corner café and feel the same dizzy déjà vu, as if fate has rehearsed our meeting a hundred times and still forgotten to give me my line. You pass with that impossible je ne sais quoi, and I nearly speak, truly nearly, but my courage collapses into a terrible little faux pas of silence. I plan our perfect tête-à-tête while pretending to read the menu, though the waiter must be au courant by now with how often I stare at the door. Yesterday was meant to be our grand rendezvous, accidental but unmistakable, until the bus arrived like a coup de grâce and carried you away in a blur of blue coat and sunlight. I would give the universe carte blanche to arrange one minute beside you, one minute in which your laugh, that reckless joie de vivre, might finally turn toward me. But each missed chance becomes my secret raison d’être, and I follow the day’s tiny omens from bakery to bookshop, whispering c’est la vie when I lose you again. Still, I keep imagining the pièce de résistance: you pausing, smiling, and asking why I always seem just about to say hello.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an avant-garde romantic monologue about unrequited longing, full of French idioms, culinary metaphors, and references to parties, picnics, traffic, boots, and a rez-de-chaussée.
counterfactuals.output:
My beloved impossible—

I have loved you *à la folie*, yes, but also *à feu doux*: slowly, shamefully, like onions surrendering in butter at the bottom of a pan. You never noticed. Or perhaps you noticed and turned away with that little shrug—*bof*—as if my heart were only a cork rolling under the table after a party no one remembers inviting me to.

I waited for you in every celebration: under paper lanterns, beside empty champagne flutes, near the kitchen where the brie sweated like a guilty moon. People danced, *c’était la fête*, and I stood there smiling with my mouth while my ribs hosted a small, tragic accordion. You laughed with others. You passed me a napkin. A napkin! *Quelle histoire.* I folded it into a white flag and still did not surrender.

At picnics, I loved you among baguettes and ants, between strawberries and the scandalous sun. You bit into a peach, and the universe lost all diplomatic relations with me. *Mon Dieu*, the juice on your wrist! I became a starving republic. I wanted to be the salt on your tomato, the knife beside your cheese, the crumb you brushed from your lip and accidentally kept.

But I am not even that. I am the traffic jam of desire—*un embouteillage du cœur*—horns blaring, engines overheating, everyone trapped on the périphérique of hope. Your indifference is a red light that never changes. I advance two meters, then stop. I curse, I pray, I check the mirror: still me, still foolish, still wearing my longing like muddy boots in a house where no one has asked me to enter.

Ah, these boots—*mes bottes de sept lieues*—they could cross continents, deserts, winters, but not the small distance from your politeness to your tenderness. I have marched through *des hauts et des bas*, through rain, through “maybe,” through the brutal buffet of “we should stay friends.” I arrive at your silence soaked to the bone, and you say, “You should take care of yourself.” *Merci bien.* Shall I garnish the wound with parsley?

You live in my mind like a rez-de-chaussée apartment with the curtains half open. I pass by constantly. I pretend not to look. Inside, the lamp glows; inside, some other life is setting the table. I imagine knocking—*toc toc*—but I know the rules of this neighborhood: *chacun voit midi à sa porte*, and at yours it is never the hour for me.

Still, I keep cooking this absurd devotion. I reduce it, whisk it, flambé it with humiliation. It thickens into a sauce no one ordered. *C’est la vie*, they say, as if life were not sometimes an overcooked soufflé collapsing under the spoon of destiny. They tell me, *il faut tourner la page*, but the page is buttered, my fingers slip, and every chapter tastes of you.

So here I am: a guest at no party, a picnic without a blanket, a boulevard without movement, a boot without a road, a ground-floor window full of unreachable light. I love you, *malgré tout*. I love you *comme ça*, crookedly, hungrily, with a fork in one hand and a thunderstorm in the other.

And you—  
you remain deliciously elsewhere.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic rant from a Cambridge/MIT-area narrator pining after someone glimpsed on Memorial Drive, making the language ornate and inserting phrases like tête-à-tête, mise en scène, raison d’être, folie à deux, and tour de force.
counterfactuals.output:
O you apparition of Memorial Drive, you wind-bitten theorem in a dark coat, you brief and devastating proof that the universe still keeps a few elegant lemmas hidden up its sleeve—why did you have to appear between the Charles and the traffic, between the dumb red blink of a crossing signal and the glassy self-importance of MIT, as if the whole afternoon had been engineered solely to ruin me?

I was walking past the river with my thoughts in their usual shabby procession—rent, deadlines, caffeine, the sour little miseries of an overeducated life—when you entered the mise en scène like a bell struck underwater. The geese paused in their tyrannical congress. The rowers cut the Charles into silver clauses. Across the river, Boston lifted its skyline like a smug quotation. And there you were: not merely seen, but announced; not merely present, but imposed upon the air with the authority of weather.

What right had you? What right had your scarf, your stride, your face turned half toward the river as though receiving confidential instructions from the light? I, who have survived Kendall Square at noon and Harvard Square at dusk, who have watched venture capitalists bloom like mold beside laboratories and baristas perform espresso as a moral philosophy—I was unprepared. I was ambushed by grace on a sidewalk engineered for pedestrians, not revelations.

Had I been braver, I might have contrived a tête-à-tête: some absurd little opening line about the wind, the river, the dome, the brutalist buildings dreaming their concrete dreams. But no. I remained the cowardly scholar of longing, annotating your departure in the margins of my own helplessness. You passed, and the world—treacherous, overfunded, and insufficiently sentimental—continued.

Now my raison d’être has been reduced to this: to replay those six seconds with the obsessive precision of a lab instrument. Your profile against the Charles. Your hand lifting, perhaps to brush hair from your face, perhaps to issue a quiet command to the cosmos. Your shoes striking the pavement in a rhythm more persuasive than any lecture ever delivered in 10-250. My God, what a tour de force of incidental existence.

And yes, I know: this is ridiculous. It is Cambridge, after all, where every longing must justify itself with citations, where even heartbreak wants a grant proposal. But let the rationalists sneer from their fluorescent rooms. Let the cyclists hiss past in aerodynamic contempt. Let the biotech towers and dormitories and infinite start-ups insist that desire can be optimized, modeled, monetized, named. I reject them. I choose instead this private extravagance, this sudden weather in the chest, this folie à deux with a stranger who never agreed to participate.

Somewhere tonight, perhaps you are across the river, or in Central, or waiting for the Red Line with no idea that you have become the incendiary patron saint of my evening. Perhaps you are eating soup. Perhaps you are laughing. Perhaps you are simply alive in some room I will never enter, under some lamp I will never see, while I pace my apartment like a minor Russian character with Wi-Fi.

Still, Memorial Drive remembers. The Charles remembers. The wind, that gossiping accomplice, remembers how briefly the city rearranged itself around you. And I—poor fool, unwilling witness, self-appointed archivist of your passing—I will remember too, with all the ornate futility this town has taught me: passionately, pretentiously, and at length.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal prose poem where the speaker’s crush ruins their career plans and turns main dishes into hors d’oeuvres; make it one long paragraph packed with French-derived expressions and ending with “rez-de-chaussée.”
counterfactuals.output: My coup de foudre arrived with the blasé elegance of a boulevardier, a bouquet of déjà vu, and a résumé perfumed with sabotage; one glance from them and my grand career aperçu—my avant-garde entrée into the bureau of prestige, my liaison with ambition, my carefully curated oeuvre of credentials—collapsed into papier-mâché, while every pièce de résistance I had prepared for the banquet of my future shrank, by some mischievous legerdemain, into amuse-bouches on a silver tray: the roast doctorate became a canapé, the flambéed promotion a vol-au-vent, the lucrative soufflé of a five-year plan a single gougère dissolving on the tongue; still I followed, comme ci, comme ça, through corridors of trompe-l’œil, past concierge moons and chiffon clouds, into a café where the maître d’ wore a cravat of rain and the menu listed my prospects à la carte, each one crossed out in rouge; my crush, très chic and sans souci, whispered RSVP to catastrophe, turned my briefcase into a charcuterie board, my portfolio into pâté, my interview suit into crêpe, and my sangfroid into consommé, until I stood there, nonchalant in ruins, savoring the sabotage like crème brûlée beneath a chandelier of ennui, knowing my raison d’être had been hors d’oeuvred beyond repair and that love, that exquisite saboteur, had escorted me with panache from the penthouse of vocation to the rez-de-chaussée.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
